1:
The chapter opens on a verb of pursuit, and Chrysostom builds his whole comment on it. A man in chase looks at nothing but the thing chased and does not leave off until he has it; and when we cannot overtake love ourselves, we may beg those nearer to hold her until we come up. She keeps escaping, he says, because we prefer everything else to her — but once she is held fast the narrow path of virtue is walked almost at leisure. Gill hears the same violence in the word, of hunting or of a pursuit to seize; Henry glosses it as a singular concern to obtain, and says the thing is to be had at any rate, whatever pains or prayers it costs.

Henry also explains why only two gifts are compared in what follows. Tongues was the gift the Corinthians valued themselves on, being the more ostentatious and the more fit to gratify pride — and the less fit for the purposes of charity, since it did not equally edify. Gifts are proper objects of desire, he grants, but in subordination to grace.

What the gift actually was is the great question of the chapter, and the witnesses divide sharply. Ellicott argues that it was not a gift of languages at all. The word for a language is used repeatedly elsewhere and never of these utterances; there is no trace of the ability ever being used to preach to foreigners, the apostles plainly not understanding the speech of Lycaonia; and the description here fits something else entirely — impassioned utterance sometimes mistaken for delirium, the expression not of thoughts but of feelings, unintelligible without interpretation and sometimes to the speaker himself. He notes that comparable phenomena have attended great revivals, and names Wesley, Whitefield and Irving. Against that, Clarke calls the chapter crowded with difficulties and prefers Lightfoot's solution: that the tongue meant is Hebrew, a dead language restored to the church, in which the scriptures were read as in the synagogue — and a man may understand a language perfectly and still be unable to expound it. Lightfoot's own argument is from plausibility: the whole Corinthian church spoke Greek, Paul is addressing its ministers and not strangers, and it is not to be believed that a minister stood up in Arabic or Armenian, from which no benefit could come to anyone — one would have to accuse him of mere foolishness or of vainglory.

A textual point underlies the whole dispute, and two witnesses press it. Ellicott and Calvin both observe that the word unknown is not in the original at all but was supplied by the seventeenth-century revisers, and that inserting it throughout the chapter quietly settles the question in favour of one theory. Calvin adds that the abuse of that rendering has done real damage.

On the effect there is no dispute. Robertson notes that the verb for understanding means simply hearing, in the sense of getting the sense rather than the sound. Calvin reaches for a proverb — the man preaches to himself and the bare walls — and takes the mysteries spoken in an unrecognised sense, as dark and involved sayings of no profit, where Chrysostom had taken them for special revelations from God. Wesley states the plain result: he speaks in effect not to men but to God, who alone understands him.
3:
Prophecy is defined by what it does. Ellicott sets the contrast in a line — communion with God by the one, communion with the brethren by the other, building up and stirring up and cheering up as each hearer requires — and Robertson glosses the three words, one of them found nowhere else in the New Testament. Calvin insists the term does not mean foretelling the future but speaking doctrine fitted to edify, the doctrine by which men are trained to piety and faith and the duties of holiness; exhortation and consolation are added because some need goads and others are pressed down. Lightfoot widens it further, to cover singing psalms as well as teaching and revelation — which, he notes, explains in what sense a woman was said earlier to prophesy. Gill puts the practical difference in one clause: the prophet preaches or prays or sings in a language the common people understand.

The comparison of the two gifts is then made by their reach. Ellicott observes that Paul's word for building up is here applied to a single man on his own account, which is unusual with him, and that the oddity is deliberate — it sharpens the antithesis between what a man does for himself and what he does for the assembly. Robertson notes a smaller thing to the same effect, that the church named as the beneficiary carries no article and means a congregation rather than the whole body.

Calvin will not let the concession to the self-edifying man stand unqualified. Whatever is done in the church ought to be for the common benefit, and where ambition makes these empty vauntings there is no real desire of doing good at all; Paul is speaking by way of concession, and in effect ordering such men of mere show out of the common society of believers. Wesley adds the same reservation in three words — the man edifies himself, and that only on the most favourable supposition.

The wish that follows is read as permission rather than desire. Lightfoot takes it as directing rather than wishing, and puts the alternative as a question that answers itself: would the apostle have them all speak in the church in Punic and Egyptian and Ethiopic and Scythian? Think seriously to what end that could be. Calvin, who does read it as a genuine commendation of languages, turns it against his own contemporaries — knowledge of tongues being at this day more than simply necessary, and God having brought them out of darkness into light, there are great theologians who declaim against them with furious zeal, and one may gather what spirit actuates such reformers. He grants at once that the cases differ: Paul had in view languages that served to publish the gospel, while these men condemn the very languages from which the pure truth of scripture must be drawn.

Paul then guards himself, and every witness marks it. Gill says the point is to keep the gift from contempt; Calvin insists God conferred nothing on his church in vain and that Paul is far from wishing tongues abolished. Clarke draws the practical comparison instead: a useful preacher unskilled in learned languages is greater in God's sight than a man with the tongues who does not interpret — and great scholars, he adds, are seldom good preachers. Ellicott notes the loophole that saves the gift: interpretation might belong to the same man, and with it tongues became as valuable to the church as prophecy.
6:
Paul puts himself in the case, and Henry draws out how much is conceded by it. An apostle with all his furniture could not edify unless he spoke to the capacity of his hearers: new revelations, the clearest explanations of old ones, the most instructive discourse in itself, are all unprofitable in a language not understood — and an exposition of scripture delivered in such a tongue would itself need expounding before it could be of any use. Gill notes that Paul was in a position to make the point about himself, having the gift as fully as any of them.

Three illustrations follow, and the witnesses are careful to keep them distinct. Ellicott insists the first is not what the English suggests: the pipe and the harp are named to show that each instrument has a sound of its own, so that you could not tell which was playing if they did not, and the question of tune belongs to the next verse. Robertson glosses the vocabulary — the word for lifeless things occurs only here, and so does the word for the pipe — and notes that the term for a distinction of sounds is the ordinary later Greek word for a difference. Clarke works the same figure the other way: tones may all be present and yet, without order or melody, nobody could discern a tune or take pleasure in the discords. Wesley reduces it to a question, what music can be made or what end answered.

The trumpet is the second and the sharpest. Ellicott states the distinction plainly — not only has each instrument its own sound, but within one instrument there are distinct notes, and a trumpet that does not clearly sound the advance or the retreat is useless because the soldiers cannot tell what to do. Clarke and Wesley both put the case as the soldier's: he is not informed, and so does not arm himself. Robertson observes that the military trumpet is louder than pipe or harp, and that the adjective for an uncertain sound means literally not manifest. Calvin, who is not usually the one to linger over antiquities, lingers here — the trumpet so rouses the spirits that it stirs not only men but horses, which is why the Lacedemonians preferred the flute when joining battle, lest the army rush on the enemy too hotly at the first charge. He grants that music has a real power over men's feelings, and cites Plato for the claim that it can shape the manners of a state.

The application is made without softening. Clarke says that a speech not understood is lost and dissipated in the air, conveying nothing, and that gifts so used are good for nothing; Robertson calls the phrase our talking to the wind, and notes that the word for speech easy to be understood means well-marked and distinct — a hint, he adds, for speakers. Wesley treats the phrase as proverbial and its meaning as the utter loss of one's labour.
10:
The third illustration widens to human speech itself. Ellicott points out that the tongue here is the physical organ, distinguished in the Greek from the tongues of the gift, and that no word in any language can be meaningless, since the thought exists first and the word is invented to express it. Gill counts the languages of the world at whatever number one likes — the Jews reckoned seventy from the confusion at Babel, and there may be more or fewer — and Clarke reads the opening words as introducing an example rather than a count, each of the tongues in question having its own articulation and emphasis and meaning. Robertson notes that the word rendered without signification means literally without the faculty of speech, and that the little clause about how many there may be is one of the rarer Greek conditional forms, meaning if it should so happen. Calvin extends the argument past men to the whole order of nature: the barking of dogs differs from the neighing of horses and the roaring of lions from the braying of asses, and every kind of bird has its own way of singing — the appointed order of things itself teaches that we must speak so as to be understood.

Then the word that ends the section. Robertson traces the term for a barbarian to the mimicking of unintelligible sound, and to the Greek habit of dividing mankind into Hellenes and everyone else; Calvin follows the same history further, through the Romans freeing themselves of the name by conquest, to Anacharsis the Scythian saying that among the Athenians the Scythians were barbarians and among the Scythians the Athenians were. No language, he concludes, is so cultivated that it is not barbarous where it is not understood. What he takes from it is a rule about speech itself: the tongue ought to be an index of the mind, an image expressing what is in the understanding — so that a man chattering in an unknown tongue is not holding fellowship with the church but keeping aloof from it, and will deservedly be despised, having first despised others. Ellicott sums the three illustrations as one argument, that the conveyance of distinct ideas is the sign and test of usefulness in each.

Paul does not tell them to stop being zealous. Clarke and Gill both note that the zeal itself is not blamed — he had told them to covet earnestly — but redirected; Robertson renders the Greek literally as zealots for spirits, which is how it looked. Ellicott reads the clause about excelling not as excelling in gifts in order to edify, but the other way about: seek the gift for the benefit of others, and by serving others you will yourselves abound. Calvin puts the same conclusion as a test — you may reckon you have attained a true and praiseworthy excellence only when the church receives advantage from you.
13:
The remedy is a prayer for the second gift. Calvin treats the verse as answering an objection that might fairly be raised — if a man can speak a foreign language, is the gift to lie useless? — and gives Paul's reply: let him ask interpretation of God as well, and until he has it, let him abstain from speaking for ostentation's sake. Ellicott notes that the Greek suggests more than a petition, hinting that the gift will be granted as well as sought; Robertson puts the alternative bluntly, that otherwise the man had better stop talking in a tongue. Clarke reads the whole thing through his Hebrew theory: let the man who reads the prophets in the original pray that he may understand them himself and be able to open their depth to others.

What Paul then means by praying with the spirit is the knot of the chapter, and Calvin says so. He rules out two older explanations — that the spirit here is the Spirit received in baptism, and Augustine's finer suggestion that it is a faculty of the soul below the understanding — and follows Chrysostom in taking it for the spiritual gift itself. Then he faces the real difficulty. We nowhere read that anyone spoke by the Spirit in a language unknown to himself; the gift was given for communication, and it would be absurd that a Roman's tongue should be framed to pronounce Greek words he did not know, as magpies and crows are taught to mimic human voices. His answer is that Paul is supposing a case for the sake of the argument, separating for illustration two things that in fact go together.

What the supposed case yields is a doctrine of prayer, and Calvin presses it hard. If the tongue is supplied with words while the mind wanders elsewhere or has no part in the business, the prayer is defective — for what else do we do in prayer but pour out our thoughts and desires before God, and what could be more at variance with a spiritual worship than that it should proceed from the lips and not from the inmost soul? He turns that against a contemporary practice with some heat: men are taught that they pray aright when their lips merely move, and unlearned people are encouraged to mutter in a language they do not understand, the intention being reckoned enough. Robertson reaches the same conclusion from the word for unfruitful, which he applies to the intellect getting no benefit from a rhapsodic prayer that may genuinely move the spirit. Ellicott adds the qualification that keeps the verse in its place: Paul is speaking of public worship throughout, and the fruitlessness in view is fruitlessness as regards others.
15:
The resolution is not to choose between the two but to have both. Gill catches the idiom of the question that introduces it, a rabbinic way of asking what is then to be done when a difficulty arises, and reads Paul's answer as refusing to lay the gift aside; Henry takes the same line, that Paul is not forbidding them to pray or sing under a divine impulse. Wesley glosses the second half as praying in a rational manner, so as not only to understand oneself but to be understood by others.

The unlearned hearer settles the question in practice. Robertson explains the word as meaning a private person, uninitiated in the gift, and locates the difficulty exactly: a man who cannot follow an ecstatic prayer will not know when to say Amen at the end of it. Ellicott makes the same point and takes the verse as evidence that congregational Amens go back to the earliest apostolic times. Clarke supplies what the response was worth to a Jewish hearer — greater, on one maxim, is he that says Amen than he that prays — and concludes that to stand in a congregation unable to say it was a serious matter. Ellicott and Clarke agree on what the next verse concedes: the thanksgiving itself was good, and it is only its public use that is being corrected.

Paul's own case closes the argument, and the witnesses read the boast as a disclaimer. Gill says he mentions it not in a boasting spirit but in humility, to show that he does not despise the gift or envy those who have it, having it more than any of them and needing it for his travels; Clarke works out which languages he must have known by education and leaves the miraculous remainder uncounted; Robertson calls it an astonishing claim that doubtless had a fine effect. And then the figure everyone remembers. Robertson notes only that private ecstasy is one thing and church worship another, and that the verb for instructing is the rare one from which catechising takes its name; Clarke states the arithmetic, that five words conveying edification are of more consequence than ten thousand that convey none. Gill is at pains to keep the number from being made to carry anything — not the five books of Moses, as Jerome suggested, and certainly not the five words of consecration on which a later doctrine was built, but simply a very few words.

Clarke closes the section with what he takes to be the key to the whole passage, borrowed from Bishop Pearce. The difficulty of the chapter lies in the two words rendered spirit and understanding, and Paul himself glosses the second here by the clause about teaching others — so that the understanding in question is the understanding the hearer has of what is said, and the spirit, standing opposite to it, is the speaker's own apprehension of what he himself utters. On that reading the whole argument falls into line, from the mysteries spoken in the spirit at the start to the five intelligible words at the end.
20:
The tone changes here, and Chrysostom explains why. After a long argument Paul turns to open rebuke, and picks an example that fits the fault: children gape after trifles and are fluttered by them, while great things move them less — and these men, having the lowest of the gifts, supposed they had everything. What he asks for is a double standard. Be children where innocence is wanted and men where understanding is; for wisdom joined to wickedness would not be wisdom, and simplicity joined to folly would not be simplicity, which is why Christ told them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.

The three words are worth separating, and Clarke and Ellicott both separate them. There are children old enough for school, infants who cannot yet speak, and men come to full growth of body and mind — and Paul assigns each a place: not schoolboys in intellect, infants in evil, grown men in understanding. Robertson renders both verbs as processes: cease becoming children in your intellects, keep on becoming adults, which he calls a needed command still. Wesley admires the stroke as oratory, bringing down their height by representing the thing they were proudest of as childishness, and adds the principle underneath it — religion was not meant to destroy any natural faculty but to exalt it, and reason in particular. Calvin turns the same verse against a use made of Christian simplicity in his own day, since Paul plainly wants believers as fully grown in understanding as they can be, and it is easier to govern the uninstructed.

The quotation that follows is the hinge, and Calvin sets it in its own context at length. The prophet is reproaching a people no more capable of instruction than children lately weaned, mimicking in his very syllables the slowness that kept them back — and the threat is that men who will not hear God speaking plainly shall hear him in the accents of a foreign army instead. That is a curse, not a favour. So the Corinthians are eagerly pursuing, as a singular benefit, the very thing God sends when he means to punish. Gill notes that the law here is not the five books but the whole of the Old Testament, which he shows to be ordinary Jewish usage; Calvin adds that the prophets had no ministry distinct from the law but were its interpreters. Henry reads the verse the same way, that tongues as the Corinthians used them were a token of judgment rather than mercy.

What follows is not an interpretation of the prophecy but a fresh thought, as Ellicott is careful to say. Tongues are a sign for unbelievers, useful to arrest attention and rouse conviction; prophecy is useful in the highest sense for those who already believe. Wesley states the same division in a line. Clarke presses the warning implicit in the quotation: what was designed as a blessing may prove a curse if the gift is used for self-aggrandisement where nobody understands it.
23:
Then the test case, and it cuts against the Corinthians twice over. Ellicott points out that if the whole church speaks in tongues the sign fails of its purpose, since the stranger drawn in by report will conclude that the assembly is mad; Robertson says they will seem a congregation of lunatics; Clarke grants that the visitor could hardly think otherwise, finding everyone talking languages that those who most needed instruction could not follow. Wesley notices a small change in the wording between the two cases — plural in the first, singular in the second — and reads something into it: several bad men together hinder one another by their talk, while single persons are more easily gained.

The reverse case is worked out step by step. Ellicott follows the sequence — one speaker after another sends something that pierces, the man is convicted in his own conscience of sin, a searching light is turned on his heart, and the secrets of it are made manifest — and Robertson glosses the two verbs as undergoing conviction and being put to the test. Clarke supplies the mechanism as he understands it: the prophets often had the discernment of spirits and could tell a man what was in his own heart, and where they had no such particular design God still led them to say the thing that suited the case before them. Wesley says only that many instances of it are seen at this day. And the end of it is worship: Ellicott takes the falling down as evidence of a complete conversion, and quotes Bengel's neat inversion of the earlier verdict — he will confess that you are not mad, but that God is truly in you. Robertson notes that the words the man is made to say are themselves a quotation, and that the sentence renders the Hebrew rather than the Greek of the prophet: really, God is in you.

Clarke draws the practical comparison the whole passage has been building to, and states it without qualification: teaching the things of God in a language men understand is of infinitely more consequence than speaking all the foreign tongues in the universe. Ellicott guards the other side of it once more — there is no danger of exaggerating the value of prophecy, since every man uttering it has something that will be useful to an outsider, which is exactly what cannot be said of the gift the Corinthians preferred.

One qualification runs through both the scenes, and Ellicott enters it twice. Neither picture is of everyone speaking at once; what is being described is the undue and exclusive cultivation of one gift by a whole congregation. He also notes that although two sorts of visitor are named — the private person without the gifts and the unbeliever — it is the second that Paul chiefly has in view, the first coming in only so far as he shares the other's inability to follow what is said.
26:
The scene is described before it is corrected. Ellicott reads the question as asking what follows from the whole argument, and notes that Paul does not answer it directly but first recalls the state of the assemblies — each man arriving with his own gift uppermost in his mind, one with a psalm, one with a discourse, one with a tongue, one with an insight, one with an interpretation. Wesley pictures the result: every one gathering a little company about him, as they did in the schools of the philosophers. Henry allows two readings, that the parts of worship were confused with one another or that several men offered the same thing at once, and asks what edification could come of such an uproar. Clarke reports Lightfoot's more orderly account, that different people wanted the time spent in different ways, but is not satisfied with it — the likelier thing is that men with extraordinary gifts each wished to put himself forward, from which confusion and perhaps contention must follow.

The rule that governs everything after is stated first. Calvin puts it as a charge to each man: let him lay out whatever gift he has for the advantage of all, the word rendered every one not implying that every last man had such a gift. Ellicott makes the same point about the occasion — in public these gifts were to be exercised not by each for himself, nor even for his own spiritual advancement, but for the building up of the whole.

Tongues are limited first. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson agree on the terms — not more than two, or at most three, in any one assembly, and those in turn rather than together, with an interpreter for the group. Calvin admires the balance of it. Paul does not set aside any gift of God, however small, so that all his benefits may be seen among believers; but he limits it so that ambition may not usurp the place due to God's glory, and so that a gift of lesser importance may not crowd out the chief ones. Wesley draws an inference about the nature of the gift from the fact that it can be scheduled at all: it seems to have been an instantaneous knowledge of a tongue, which a man could afterwards speak when he thought fit, without a new miracle each time.

Without an interpreter the rule is absolute. Robertson notes that the imperative is continuous — he is not to speak in a tongue even once — and that he may still indulge his ecstasy privately. Calvin reads the alternative as thanksgiving rather than mere private exercise: let the man recognise the favour in his own mind with gratitude and enjoy it as his own when there is no opportunity of bringing it forward publicly.
29:
Prophecy is limited next, and Calvin notices that the number is the same. He explains the apparent oddity — if tongues are the less useful, why not a smaller allowance? — by observing that interpretation stood in the place of prophecy, so the two counts are not really parallel; and he adds a plainer reason for any limit at all, that multitude breeds confusion, and that continued application to prophesying would in itself be the most desirable thing of all. What he chiefly wants is that the less skilful should not prevent the better qualified from being heard, since none are more inclined to push themselves forward than those with a slight smattering of learning.

What the silent ones are to do is not nothing. Ellicott and Robertson both take the judging as a testing of whether the utterance is from the Spirit of God, and Ellicott adds the mechanics of the interruption: if a revelation came suddenly to a man sitting by, the speaker gave way, the suddenness itself showing that the truth was needed then and there. Clarke traces the practice to the synagogue, where objecting and interrogating and refuting were customary, and gives the reason for caution — a man might claim the spirit of prophecy without being sent, so the accredited teachers had to examine whether what was said agreed with truth. Calvin faces the obvious objection, that the doctrine of God ought to be beyond controversy: the answer is that it is not men's scrutiny that is permitted but a judging by the Spirit, whether what is set before them is God's word or human invention passed off under that name.

The last two verses give the ground of the whole arrangement. Ellicott anticipates the excuse — that the rushing Spirit overcame them and they could not help themselves — and says Paul's reply is simply that they can, the spirits of the prophets being under the prophets' control. Wesley presses the contrast with the heathen priests, whose possession forced them to speak and act like madmen, while the Spirit of God left his prophets the clear use of their judgment about when and how long to speak. Clarke puts it in five words: God grants no ungovernable gifts. And Robertson, Clarke and Ellicott all take the closing sentence as the principle behind every rule in the chapter — the church should bear the moral image of its King, so that disorder cannot be laid at his door, and orderly reverence is the mark of the churches.
34:
The section belongs where it stands, and Chrysostom explains the sequence. Having quieted the disturbance from the tongues and from the prophesyings, and made a rule to keep either from breaking in on the other, Paul turns to a third disorder; and he does it opportunely, since if men with genuine gifts may not speak inconsiderately or whenever they please, still less may others. Ellicott joins the closing words of the previous verse to this one, so that the appeal to the practice of all the churches introduces the rule rather than concluding what went before — the example of every other congregation being against what was happening at Corinth.

What is being forbidden is the question, and the witnesses answer it differently. Clarke restricts it narrowly. The Jewish synagogue allowed any man to ask questions, object, and attempt a refutation, and allowed no woman to do so; Paul carries the same rule into the church, and what he opposes is the questioning and fault-finding and disputing, together with the attempt to set one's judgment against another's in public. Clarke is explicit that this leaves the earlier chapter standing: where a woman received a particular influence from God enabling her to teach, she was to obey it, and Paul had already given directions for her appearance when so employed. He supports the reading from the harshness of what the rabbis had said — one of them that the words of the law should sooner be burned than delivered to women — and takes the gospel to have changed that, the Spirit being poured out on women as well as men according to the prophecy of Joel.

Henry and Calvin read it more broadly. Henry takes the prohibition to cover praying and prophesying alike, understanding prophecy in this chapter's restricted sense of preaching or interpreting scripture by inspiration; he grants that the earlier chapter seems to assume women did sometimes pray and prophesy in the assemblies, and that Paul there condemned the manner rather than the thing, but here he thinks the public performance itself is forbidden. Calvin argues from incompatibility: teaching is a position of superiority in the church, and it would be unseemly that one who is under subjection to a member should preside over the whole body. He enters one large qualification, however — this concerns ordinary service in a regularly constituted church, and a necessity may arise of such a kind as to require that a woman should speak in public. He adds a second at the end, that the matters treated here are things indifferent, in which nothing is unlawful except what is at variance with propriety and edification.

Chrysostom and Ellicott both trace the appeal to the law back to the sentence in Genesis rather than to any statute; Chrysostom notes that Paul does not say let them be silent but something stronger, that they be in subjection. Wesley enters the same exception Calvin does, and enters it in his first clause: unless they are under an extraordinary impulse of the Spirit.

Robertson is the one witness who takes the difficulty head on rather than resolving it. He says there is no doubt what Paul means here, and no doubt either that some women were disturbing the worship; but he sets beside it that the daughters of Philip were prophetesses, that modern Christians have concluded these commands were meant for conditions that do not wholly apply now, that women do most of the teaching in the Sunday schools of his own day, and that the line is not easy to draw. His conclusion is a request rather than a ruling: that we be patient with one another as we try to understand what Paul really meant.
35:
The provision about asking at home is read as a concession, not a further restriction. Calvin is careful that it should not shut women out of learning, and notes that Paul does not forbid consulting the prophets themselves where a husband is not competent to answer — the point being to keep a disputation out of the assembly, not to keep the question unanswered. Ellicott and Wesley say the same more briefly. Clarke adds the synagogue parallel once more, that a woman was not suffered to read there though a servant or a child might, and repeats that the conduct in view is the conduct that proved they were not under obedience.

Chrysostom anticipates the obvious objection and answers it in a sentence. If they are not even to speak or ask a question, someone will say, to what end are they present at all? That they may hear what they ought — and the points they want cleared up let them learn at home. It is the same answer Calvin gives, from the other direction: the aim is not to leave the question unanswered but to keep the disputation out of the assembly.

Clarke reads the word for shame narrowly, of the conduct rather than of the sex, and takes it as further evidence that what is in view throughout is the disorderly and disobedient, not any woman on whom God had poured out his Spirit. Wesley marks only the place and the persons — that is where such enquiry belongs, and those are the people to make it of.

Henry gives the rebuke that follows its edge. The Corinthians managed their gifts as no other church did, behaved in a manner by themselves, and would not easily endure regulation — and the two questions Paul asks are meant to beat that down. Did the gospel come out from them? Or did it come to them only? Neither question can be answered in a way that leaves them free to make their own rules: they neither originated the message nor received it alone, and the practice of every other congregation therefore has a claim on them. It is the same argument the section opened with, when the custom of all the churches of the saints was set against what was being done at Corinth, and Paul has simply brought it round again in the form of a question they must answer themselves.
37:
The claim Paul makes for his own instructions is unusually direct, and the witnesses say so. Ellicott calls it the clearest and most emphatic statement of his claim to inspiration anywhere, and notes the test proposed with it: the best evidence a man could give of possessing these gifts would be conduct the opposite of what they seemed to think the gifts entitled them to. Robertson observes who would be quick to resent the sharpness — the prophet, the speaker in tongues, the disturbing woman — and that Paul meets them by claiming inspiration for his position. Clarke reads the sentence as self-testing: the truly spiritual man will acknowledge that this comes from the same Spirit.

Calvin sets the claim in the frame of the chapter itself. The judging he had assigned to the prophets is exactly what he now invites — not that his doctrine should be treated as doubtful, but that they should recognise it as God's word if they judge rightly. He also enters two cautions. Such confidence was allowable for Paul, who was assured of his revelation and well enough known to the Corinthians, but it is not for everyone to advance the claim, and a man who does will earn derision by his boasting unless the thing shows itself in reality. And when he asks how rules of external order can be called commandments of the Lord, when scripture prescribes no such rites, his answer is careful: God gave Paul the wisdom to recommend this order, not as an inviolable law like those governing the worship of God, but as a useful directory not to be despised.

The next sentence is textually uncertain, and Ellicott gives both readings with equal weight — either that a man who will not recognise so plain a truth may be left in his ignorance, or that the man who does not know this is himself not known, that is, not known of God. Calvin takes the first and reads it as a refusal to be drawn: sceptics and contentious persons do not diminish the authority of sound doctrine by the questions they raise, and their doubts should be no hindrance to us. He guards it at once — that elevation of mind which despises human judgments must rest on ascertained truth, or it is mere perverse rashness. Clarke compresses the whole into five words: let him be so at his peril.

The summing-up puts the two gifts back in their order. Ellicott notes that the phrasing itself carries the relative valuation Paul has been urging and the Corinthians had inverted — earnestly seek the one, and do not forbid the other. Clarke says the same and adds the reason for the second half: let no gift envy another, nor prevent a man doing the work God has qualified him for. Calvin makes the not-forbidding a matter of divesting oneself of envy and allowing others the praise due to a rarer gift.

The last verse is read as the principle behind everything. Clarke takes the two words apart — in their proper forms, with becoming reverence, and then everything in its place and its time — and remarks that the manner of doing a thing is often what gives the act all its use. Ellicott makes the same point about permanence: the particular circumstances that called out these instructions passed away centuries ago, but the principle abides, and by it he judges both the outbursts of incoherent fanaticism that have recurred in the church's history and the practice of conducting public services in a tongue the people do not understand.
